title: How to evaluate holographic setup stability?

posts.topic_title: How to evaluate holographic setup stability?
posts.author: Cristiano_Perrucci
posts.post_subject: How to evaluate holographic setup stability?
posts.content_md:
Hi all,

after a couple of day spent workin hard on my new holo bench, I tested the new setup with interferometer.

Well, the working area seems to be quite stable, fringes are well visible and, without strong vibration causes such as train or buses, no fringes movements are apreciable.

But...when goods trains runs along the railwail or buses jumps on the road, fringes start to slip. The fringes slips are quick and just a few seconds are needed to recover bench stability.

The questions are:

-How much is the maximum allowable fringe movement without affecting the hologram quality?

- How to calculate the relative path difference using a Mitchelson interf. assuming this difference <1 lambda ?

Hoping these question are't too dummy...

Thanks,

Cristiano

posts.post_subject: How to evaluate holographic setup stability?
posts.content_md:
First you will want to look here:

[http://www.holographyforum.org/HoloWiki ... rferometry](http://www.holographyforum.org/HoloWiki/index.php/Interferometry)

You will need to have the fringes lock to 1/4 of a fringe or better. Use a pencil to mark a fringe and make sure it returns to the same place after a train goes by. If it does you will not do as bad as if it rests in a new place.

Also, this was added this weekend by wler:

[http://www.holographyforum.org/HoloWiki ... nce_Length](http://www.holographyforum.org/HoloWiki/index.php/Equipment#Longitudinal_Modes_and_Coherence_Length)

posts.topic_title: How to evaluate holographic setup stability?
posts.author: BobH
posts.post_subject: How to evaluate holographic setup stability?
posts.content_md:
> -How much is the maximum allowable fringe movement without affecting the hologram quality?

Depends on the recording material in use, and exposure times. If using silver halide and with a long exposure time (say 2 minutes), a transient vibration of a few seconds which settles back to the original position of the fringes is OK. If the exposure time is 10 seconds, a 5 second long transient vibration will give a very bad result.

Fringe drift is way more damaging to a recording than vibrations caused by busses or trains because if it's there, it's always there. If the fringes start in one place and finish in another, regardless of exposure time, a bad hologram will result.
